extracted.intended_audience: journalists, public relations professionals, politicians, students, and general readers interested in apologies and reputation management
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing and classifying 'non-apology' statements (forms of apology that avoid remorse or responsibility), their rhetorical forms, legal significance, and tactical uses in politics and public relations. Useful for analyzing public statements, press releases, and crisis communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-apology definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-apology ... is a statement in the form of an apology that does not express remorse for what was done or said, or assigns fault to those ostensibly receiving the apology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in politics and public relations; it takes the form of an apology but fails to acknowledge responsibility or genuine remorse. Example formulation: 'I'm sorry you feel that way.' Use this definition to judge whether a given statement is an apology in form only or a genuine acceptance of fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'I'm sorry you feel that way' / blaming the recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying 'I'm sorry you feel that way' is a non-apology: it does not admit there was anything wrong with the remarks made, and blames the recipient by implying they were overly sensitive or took offense for irrational reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such statements as defensive rather than conciliatory. They deflect responsibility and may inflame rather than soothe offended parties. Use as an indicator that the speaker is avoiding admission of wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic apology to 'anyone who might have been offended'
rubrics_metrics.description: An apology that does not apologize directly to the injured or insulted party, but generically 'to anyone who might have been offended'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form avoids addressing the harmed party and sidesteps responsibility. It signals an attempt to appear conciliatory without committing to specific remediation or acknowledgement of harm; mark as a distancing tactic in evaluation of sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional 'if' apology (ifpology)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'if' apology: lines such as 'I apologize if I offended anyone' — sometimes called an ifpology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding 'if' or similar conditional modifiers makes the apology contingent and is characterized as a non-apology by commentators and experts (e.g., John Kador). Use of 'if' signals the speaker is not admitting that offense actually occurred or that they caused it; treat as weak or non-sincere apology in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Mistakes were made' / passive-voice evasive phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression 'mistakes were made' is a rhetorical device using the passive voice to acknowledge poor handling while evading any direct admission of responsibility by omitting who made the mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect passive constructions that abstract or anonymize responsibility ('mistakes were made') as classic examples of non-apology language. An active alternative ('I made mistakes' or 'John Doe made mistakes') indicates acceptance of responsibility; penalize passive-evasive phrasing when assessing sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-apology that expresses regret without responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements of pseudo-apology that do not communicate responsibility for words or deeds may be meaningful expressions of regret, but such statements can also be used to elicit forgiveness without acknowledging fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the dual nature: such statements may placate offended parties yet leave underlying accountability unaddressed. When evaluating an apology, separate expressed regret from admission of responsibility and look for commitments to change or remediation to assess genuineness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology: Tactical apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactical apology — when a person accused of wrongdoing offers an apology that is rhetorical and strategic—and not necessarily heartfelt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to defuse situations or validate feelings without accepting blame (e.g., airlines apologizing for delays). In evaluations, label apologies that prioritize damage control over contrition as tactical and consider their likely efficacy and ethical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology: Explanation apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation apology — when a person accused of wrongdoing offers an apology that is merely a gesture that is meant to counter an accusation of wrongdoing; in fact, it may be used to defend the actions of the accused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form provides context or justification alongside a token apology. When assessing, check whether the explanation serves to minimize responsibility or to genuinely explain and accept error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology: Formalistic apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalistic apology — when a person accused of wrongdoing offers an apology after being admonished to do so by an authority figure—who may also be the individual who suffered the wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often ritualistic and performed to satisfy external demand rather than to express remorse. Evaluate such apologies for authenticity and for whether they are accompanied by substantive corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology: Happy ending apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Happy ending apology — when a person accused of wrongdoing fully acknowledges responsibility for the wrongdoing and is genuinely remorseful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents the sincere, full apology that includes acceptance of responsibility and often promises of change. Non-apology forms are unsuited to contexts where a happy ending apology is required (e.g., serious harm). Use this as the positive benchmark when judging apology quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success measured by outcome rather than degree of contrition
rubrics_metrics.description: Typologies of apology note ... success is to be gauged by the result of the apology rather than the degree of contrition involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an apology, consider practical outcomes (restoration, forgiveness, reduced tension) in addition to expressed emotion. A tactical apology may be judged successful if it accomplishes necessary social repair despite limited contrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal significance: avoiding litigation through non-apology (United States)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-apology apologizers may be trying to avoid litigation that might result from an admission of guilt or responsibility. Many states, including Massachusetts and California, have laws to prevent a plaintiff from using an apology as evidence of liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In legal-risk contexts (healthcare, litigation), recognize that non-apologies can be deliberate risk management. Note statutory protections in some U.S. states that allow apologies without admitting liability; this influences organizational apology strategy and how statements should be interpreted legally vs. ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apology statutes in Canada (Alberta and British Columbia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alberta's Evidence Act section 26.1 provides that an apology does not constitute an express or implied admission of fault or liability; British Columbia passed similar legislation in 2006 (Apology Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing apologies from Canadian actors, account for statutory protections that separate expressions of apology/regret from legal admissions. This affects whether organizations choose to apologize and how that apology is likely to be construed in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apology as a negotiation and de-escalation tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiators often use this tactic to calm tense situations: 'an apology can defuse emotions effectively, even when you do not acknowledge personal responsibility for the action or admit an intention to harm. An apology may be one of the least costly and most rewarding investments you can make.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat apologies (including tactical or non-apology forms) as tools to manage emotions and negotiation dynamics. Evaluate their effectiveness by whether they reduce hostility and enable constructive dialogue, even when responsibility isn't admitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sarcastic or humorous 'perfect non-apology' constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous or sarcastic 'non-apology' constructions (e.g., Bruce McCall's 'The Perfect Non-apology Apology') demonstrate 'double talk' designed to seem regretful while accepting no blame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use satirical examples to illustrate how language can be engineered to appear apologetic without accountability. These are instructive as anti-patterns when teaching or assessing authentic apology language.
